title: Prepare an Older Lighting System Review from Existing Records
description: Separate existing installation records, dated observations and proposed changes before requesting a review of an older lighting system.
articleHtml:
Identify what the review should answer

An installation described as older does not, by that description alone, establish which equipment is present, what condition it is in or which changes should follow. Start an enquiry with the question you want answered: understanding the existing installation, discussing a reported change, or considering a different use of an outdoor area. Keep these questions separate so a proposed redesign does not become an assumed repair diagnosis.

Keep installation history attached to its source

List the records already available, such as a dated proposal, an equipment list or a later service note. Identify which document supplied each detail. An original proposal describes a proposed scope; without further evidence it does not establish that every listed item was installed or remains present. A later note may concern only one part of the installation.

Where an installation date, model reference or later change is unknown, leave it unknown. A photograph of a label already available in your records can be described as a reference for review, rather than confirmation of compatibility or present equipment condition. Avoid filling gaps with an assumed standard configuration.

Separate observations from requested changes

Describe an observation with its date and source. “The owner reported a different appearance on June 14” and “a replacement was requested on June 15” are different statements. The second does not demonstrate why the first occurred. Identify whether a note came from your own observation, another person's report or an existing document.

For a fictional example, an original proposal names three areas, a later note names one fixture, and the current enquiry asks about using a new seating area. Those records support three different questions: what was proposed, what the later note covers, and what the owner now wants considered. They do not establish an equipment count, a fault or a suitable replacement.

Ask for a defined review scope

State which areas and questions you want included. Ask what information would be needed to assess continued use, a repair enquiry or a proposed layout change. Keep an estimate request distinct from an accepted scope, and record any unanswered questions about exclusions or additional assessment.

This is a way to organize an enquiry, not an inspection or an equipment recommendation. No property, installation, service agreement or equipment condition was inspected for this guide. It establishes no compatibility, replacement benefit, electrical procedure, professional assessment, service availability or booking outcome.

Questions before sending the enquiry

Does an older installation automatically need replacement?

The age description alone does not establish condition or an appropriate next step. Ask for a review tied to the identified installation and the question you want answered.

Can an original proposal serve as the current equipment inventory?

Keep it identified as an original proposal. Ask which details need confirmation before treating it as a record of equipment currently present.

How should an uncertain installation date be recorded?

Mark the date as unknown and identify any dated documents separately. A document date is not automatically the installation date.

Does a requested change confirm a repair diagnosis?

No. Record the requested change separately from the reported observation and leave the cause unresolved unless an appropriate assessment establishes it.
